title: FPRAS for counting undirected Euler tours
formal:
Does the number of Euler tours of an arbitrary connected Eulerian undirected graph admit a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme? Using the labelled-edge, fixed-first-traversal normalization below, let \(Z(G)\) be the tour count. The question is whether there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,a>0\) such that, for every allowed graph \(G\) and every integer \(q\ge2\), the algorithm outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) in at most \(C(N+q+1)^a\) bit operations on every random tape and
\[\Pr\!\left[\left|\widehat Z-Z(G)\right|\le\frac{Z(G)}q\right]\ge\frac34.\]
Here \(N\) is the input encoding length and the probability is over the algorithm’s independent fair random bits. The constants are independent of the graph and accuracy. There is no degree bound, planarity promise or prescribed sampling chain.
why: Euler tours are elementary graph traversals whose existence is easy to decide, yet approximate enumeration remains a major counting question. A solution would clarify how much harder it is to impose one globally connected traversal than to satisfy local balance constraints on edge directions. This is a test case for the reach of randomized approximate counting beyond problems with tractable orientation or matching formulations.

sentences: An Euler tour traverses every edge of an undirected graph exactly once and returns to its start.
This question asks whether the number of such tours can be approximated by a randomized algorithm in fully polynomial time.
The count uses labelled edges and a fixed first traversal to remove rotation and reversal ambiguity.
The accuracy is multiplicative, and the success probability must be at least three quarters on every input.
Known orientation-counting algorithms and restricted graph results do not resolve the general tour-counting question.

definitions:
A graph has labelled vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge1\), and labelled edges \(E=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct endpoints. Parallel edges are permitted and remain distinct by their labels; there are no loops. The graph is promised connected, and every vertex has even degree, counting parallel edges with their multiplicities. The input explicitly lists every edge, rather than encoding a multiplicity by a large binary number. One encoding uses unary \(n\), self-delimiting binary \(m\), the endpoint pair of each edge in label order, and self-delimiting binary \(q\). Graphs are unweighted.

If \(m>0\), write the endpoints of edge 1 as \(a_1<b_1\). Define \(Z(G)\) to be the number of sequences
\[v_0,e_1,v_1,e_2,v_2,\ldots,e_m,v_m\]
such that \((e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) is a permutation of all edge labels, \(e_1=1\), \(v_0=a_1\), \(v_1=b_1\), \(v_m=v_0\), and edge \(e_i\) joins \(v_{i-1}\) to \(v_i\) for every \(i\). Vertices may be revisited; edges may not. This fixes the starting point and traversal direction by the first labelled edge. It counts one representative of each closed tour modulo cyclic rotation and reversal, while retaining vertex and edge labels. No quotient by graph automorphisms is taken. For the single-vertex graph with no edges, put \(Z(G)=1\), counting the empty tour.

The allowed nonempty graphs have Euler tours. Allowing explicit parallel edges is compatible with the usual simple-graph formulation: replacing each labelled edge by a path through its own new degree-two vertex preserves the tour count under the corresponding first-edge convention and increases the input size only polynomially. Thus this representation choice does not demand a different approximation complexity.

The output is a pair of binary integers specifying a nonnegative rational with positive denominator. Its writing and all arithmetic are charged in the standard multitape Turing model; neither large integers nor rational operations have unit cost. All choices of random bits terminate within the stated bound. A bad random tape may give an inaccurate estimate, but the displayed success probability holds separately for every graph and accuracy input.

The accuracy \(1/q\) is relative to the count. It covers arbitrary requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) by taking \(q\ge\max\{2,1/\varepsilon\}\). Runtime is polynomial in \(q\), not merely polynomial in graph size for each fixed accuracy. The fixed success threshold \(3/4\) is the convention inherited from the card. No particular estimator, Markov chain or proof technique is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm meeting all displayed guarantees, or a Lean-checked proof of the negation of that existence statement. A positive answer must approximate the normalized tour count on every allowed Eulerian graph in fully polynomial time. An exact-counting hardness theorem alone does not refute an FPRAS. Counting balanced orientations, solving a fixed-degree or fixed-grid-width subcase, or proving convergence of a sampler without a fully polynomial approximation guarantee is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Cryan’s 2024 abstract says that an FPRAS remains unknown even for undirected 4-regular graphs. It discusses rapid mixing for a particular two-row toroidal-grid chain, a restricted graph family. The full card asks for an algorithm on arbitrary Eulerian graphs.

Ge and Štefankovič explicitly state the general-graph FPRAS question. Their exact-counting results include hardness on planar 4-regular graphs, but exact hardness is not an approximation lower bound. Their introduction carefully separates exact reductions from approximation-preserving reductions.

The same paper gives an approximation-preserving reduction to counting A-trails in 4-regular maps. Such a map supplies a cyclic order of incident edges, and an A-trail requires consecutive traversed edges to be adjacent in that order. That additional model is distinct from ordinary tours on a 4-regular graph and is not silently substituted into this question.

An Eulerian orientation assigns one direction to each edge so that indegree equals outdegree at every vertex. The cited sampling notes prove an FPRAS for these orientations. An orientation records edge directions but not their traversal order, so its count is a different target from the number of tours.
